ats_best_practices.content: ATS Formatting Best Practices: Use standard section headings (Experience, Education, Skills, Summary). Avoid tables, columns, headers, footers, and text boxes. Use standard bullet points (•). Do not use images, graphics, or icons. Use standard fonts (Arial, Calibri, Times New Roman). Save as PDF or DOCX. Keep file size under 2MB. Use simple formatting with consistent spacing.

ATS Keyword Optimization: Mirror exact keywords from the job description. Use both acronyms and full forms (e.g., 'Machine Learning (ML)'). Place critical keywords in the first half of the resume. Include keywords in context, not just listed. Use industry-standard terminology. Include both hard skills and soft skills from the JD. Repeat important keywords 2-3 times naturally throughout the resume.

ATS Section Completeness: A complete resume must have: Contact Information (name, email, phone, location, LinkedIn), Professional Summary (2-4 sentences), Work Experience (company, title, dates, bullet points), Education (degree, institution, graduation date), Skills (technical and soft skills). Optional but recommended: Projects, Certifications, Publications. Missing sections reduce ATS scores significantly.

ATS Bullet Point Quality: Start every bullet with a strong action verb. Include quantifiable metrics (percentages, dollar amounts, user counts, time saved). Follow the STAR method (Situation, Task, Action, Result). Keep bullets to 1-2 lines maximum. Use past tense for previous roles, present tense for current role. Avoid personal pronouns (I, me, my). Each bullet should demonstrate impact, not just describe duties.

Common ATS Mistakes to Avoid: Using creative job titles instead of standard ones. Putting important info in headers/footers (ATS can't read them). Using abbreviations without spelling them out first. Having spelling errors or typos. Using fancy templates with graphics. Not tailoring resume for each job application. Listing responsibilities instead of achievements. Having employment gaps without explanation. Using outdated or irrelevant skills.
